title: How Steadicams Work
summary: Hosts discuss the Steadicam, the handheld stabilizing camera rig invented by Garrett Brown. They cover the film-making problems that preceded it (dollies, stairs, rough terrain), Brown's sizzle reel of impossible shots, early films that used it (Bound for Glory, Rocky, Marathon Man, The Shining, Goodfellas, Return of the Jedi), and how the vest, arm, sled, and gimbal work using counterbalance and moment of inertia. They also touch on consumer stabilizers, Skycam, and listener mail.
topics: Return of the Jedi speeder bike

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts chat about Josh's lost Last Chance Garage hat and replacement patches.

segments.title: Steadicam operators and film sets
segments.summary: The hosts discuss why Steadicam rigs are rarely used on their own shows, that operators are paid for with the package, and that the skill is different from other camera roles.

segments.title: Garrett Brown and pre-Steadicam limits
segments.summary: Garrett Brown, a commercial camera operator, grew frustrated by roughly thirty shots that were impossible with the equipment of the day, such as stairs and rough terrain. Handheld shots looked jarring and avant-garde at the time.

segments.title: Balance, the vestibular system, and dollies
segments.summary: The hosts explain how the human inner ear and retina offset motion, and describe the dolly as a heavy wheeled sled on track that limits where a camera can go.

segments.title: The sizzle reel and Kubrick's shadow note
segments.summary: Brown made a sizzle reel of the impossible shots, including a swimming pool scene and a shot of his wife on the Philadelphia Museum of Art steps. Stanley Kubrick warned him that shadows in the reel revealed the rig, and Brown cut those shots from the second edition.

segments.title: Early films: Rocky, Bound for Glory, and the Steadicam's debut
segments.summary: The Museum steps shot reportedly inspired John G. Avildsen to use it in Rocky. In 1976 Brown operated on several major films, including Bound for Glory, which used a crane-to-ground smooth shot. The patent was pending until 1977 and Brown won a Technical Achievement Academy Award in 1978.

segments.title: How the Steadicam works: vest, arm, and sled
segments.summary: The rig has three parts: a vest, a spring-and-pulley arm that redistributes the camera weight, and a sled with a stage and pole. The camera can be in high mode or low mode. Josh's brother built a homemade version from door hinges and springs.

segments.title: Center of gravity, gimbal, and moment of inertia
segments.summary: Brown spread the camera's components along a pole so the center of gravity sits on the pole, with a gimbal above it. The hosts compare this to balancing a broomstick on a finger and explain moment of inertia and how the arm isolates the operator's movement.

segments.title: Operating the Steadicam on set and the Eurovision shot
segments.summary: Operators need breaks because of the weight. A Eurovision shot showed an operator on a Segway circling a singer, and the hosts compare the event to American Idol.

segments.title: Transition to famous shots
segments.summary: Hosts introduce a discussion of famous Steadicam shots.

segments.title: Famous Steadicam shots: The Shining, Goodfellas, Return of the Jedi
segments.summary: The Shining's maze and tricycle shots are discussed, along with the Goodfellas Copacabana tracking shot and lighting challenges. Return of the Jedi's speeder bike chase used Garrett Brown walking slowly, sped up on film. Kubrick and Brown reportedly clashed on The Shining.

segments.title: Consumer stabilizers and Steadicam brands
segments.summary: Consumer options include a roughly one hundred dollar GoPro rig and the Smoothie for iPhone. Gimbal drones are also mentioned. Tiffen makes Steadicam; Glidecam and Easyrig are rival brands. Chapman and Fisher make dollies.

segments.title: Skycam and camera position names
segments.summary: Brown later invented the Skycam, a cable-suspended camera used in football. Hosts describe the forward and backward operator positions, nicknamed missionary and don Juan.

segments.title: Listener mail from Dane in Minnesota
segments.summary: A Christian listener praises the show's handling of religious topics and sensitive subjects like satanic panic.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give social media and website information and sign off.
